content:
A New Jersey-based theater company is defending its plans for an album titled “George Floyd the Musical” after being hit with heated backlash from Broadway actors and other members of the performing arts community.

On Thursday, theater publication Playbill posted a statement on its social media platforms apologizing for running a job listing attributed to the theater company Busted Broadway of West Milford, New Jersey, that sought “comedic singers and musical theater vocal talent” for recording sessions for “George Floyd the Musical.”

“Late yesterday afternoon, Playbill Jobs incorrectly approved a job listing that had no place on our site,” the outlet wrote. “Once leadership was alerted, the listing was immediately removed, and we began reviewing and revising our approval processes.”

The statement continued: “We apologize unequivocally for giving this hateful listing any further air, and we promise to do better going forward. We at Playbill aim to lift up this community with empathy, consideration, and respect. We hope those who read and follow us do the same.”

In a separate statement, Playbill chairman Philip Birsh and chief operating officer Alex Birsh said they were “terribly crestfallen that our system to catch inappropriate and offensive submissions failed to catch this outrageous posting,” noting that Busted Broadway would be banned from their site’s job listings page going forward.

“The people and company responsible for this unseemly and grotesque submission will not benefit from their prank or strategy of all media is good media,” the statement continued, per Deadline. “While a Playbill employee made the error of approving this offensive job posting, the person who wrote that job description and the company behind this outrage and submission to Playbill deserves harsh scrutiny. They also do not deserve to be a part of our world any further.”

In it, Busted Broadway says it emphasizes “dark, subversive, edgy, and controversial issues” in its productions, and urges those who are “uncomfortable performing offensive material” not to audition for the project.

The ad garnered widespread attention after being called out by actor and singer Malynda Hale in an Instagram post.

“I really don’t like to participate in outrage culture,” she wrote in the caption, “but this is so outrageously disrespectful I truly have to ask HAS EVERYONE LOST THEIR DAMN MINDS?!”

Hale’s video drew a flurry of responses from fellow performers, including actors Viola Davis and Donna Murphy.

“I mean……WHAAT??!!! I would’ve lived to have been in the room when this one was pitched!” Davis wrote in the comments.

Noted Murphy: “Ummm… if this is a real thing- DISGUSTING & DISTURBING. If it’s not - still completely horrendous & offensive. WTF.”

Aside from the title, the listing gave no indication as to how the musical intended to depict its subject matter. Floyd was a 46-year-old Black man whose 2020 murder by Minneapolis police drew nationwide protests.

Derek Chauvin was immediately fired from his police role after being caught on video kneeling on Floyd’s neck for around nine minutes, killing him. In 2021, the former officer was convicted of two counts of murder and one count of manslaughter, receiving 22.5 years in prison. He’s since received an additional 21-year sentence, to be served concurrently, for violating Floyd’s civil rights.

On Thursday afternoon, Broadway Busted issued a statement on its social media platforms clarifying that the musical was intended as a “satire on the culture” rather than a realistic depiction of the events surrounding Floyd’s death.

“Never judge a show by its title, as many who have never seen the script or score appear to be doing now,” the statement continued.

On its website, Busted Broadway says it is “devoted to the funny, absurd, and ridiculous humor baked into our collective human condition” and “not for the mollycoddled or politically correct listener.”

One of Busted Broadway’s founders is Kevin Lynch, a white musician who last December filed a lawsuit accusing the off-Broadway theater company Playwrights Horizons of “discriminatory pricing” when it hosted a “BIPOC Night,” offering discounted tickets for Black audience members and other patrons of color.

According to The New York Times, the suit was resolved out of court in May, though it was never specified whether the theater paid any money to Lynch.
